This simulator utilizes continuous-time memristive models to accurately capture the dynamics of devices and multi-device interactions. NARS allows for the creation and simulation of neuromorphic networks within an interface, providing a comprehensive understanding of system behavior. The software's versatility supports various memristive models and devices, offering researchers a valuable tool to explore and investigate neuromorphic systems with greater ease. This article details NARS's underlying memristive models, functionality, implementation, validation, performance, and potential applications in neuromorphic research. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a prominent method for training agents in the field of reinforcement learning. However, agents trained using MLE often prioritize short-term goals over long-term ones, which can be rectified by implementing a bias towards the desired long-term rewards. This study proposes a novel approach called Reward-Biased MLE (RBMLE), which enhances agent performance by incorporating a reward bias. RBMLE can be applied to a broad range of reinforcement learning algorithms and has been successfully integrated with neural contextual agents. The results of agent evaluations demonstrate that RBMLE consistently outperforms conventional MLE in terms of long-term credit assignment and reward exploration. RBMLE is also shown to be a more efficient technique compared to maximum entropy approaches, as it can achieve similar effects at lower computational costs. Moreover, RBMLE enables agents to learn complex behaviors involving high degrees of exploration without requiring explicit entropy regularization. The study concludes by highlighting potential areas for further research, including the adaptation of RBMLE for real-world applications and exploring alternative methods for implementing reward biases. This research aims to demonstrate how statistical physics and machine learning can be used together to better understand intricate social systems by examining a specific example - the spread of infectious diseases. Two prominent researchers in this field, E. Lerner and D. Goldenbaum, discuss the challenges that typically arise when studying social systems: the scarcity of reliable data, the difficulty of accurately modeling the systems, and the limited effectiveness of traditional computational approaches. To overcome these obstacles, the researchers propose a novel methodology that combines statistical physics and machine learning to create a predictive computational framework for complex systems. This approach is illustrated through a case study on predicting disease transmission by applying it to data from the 1918 pandemic. The methodology's key components include: (i) using statistical physics to develop a simplified model that captures the essential characteristics of the system, (ii) using machine learning to create a predictive model that can make accurate forecasts, and (iii) using machine learning to create a data generator that can produce synthetic data to complement real-world data. Ultimately, the researchers demonstrate that this approach enables the creation of accurate predictive models even when working with limited data. The methodology's potential to better understand and model social systems is also explored in the context of other significant social phenomena, such as the spread of infectious diseases and the emergence of collective behavior. Additionally, the researchers discuss the broader implications of this approach for addressing pressing issues, such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. This research aims to provide a foundation for future studies on the application of statistical physics and machine learning to better understand and model social systems. Visual metaphors, a powerful way to convey meaning through a combination of words and images, have been given limited attention in research, particularly when it comes to automatically understanding their meaning. Current approaches focus on either generating metaphors or interpreting them, but a comprehensive, multi-faceted dataset to drive progress in visual metaphor research is lacking. We aim to bridge this gap by introducing MetaCLUE, a large, diverse collection of 12,000 manually annotated visual metaphors, covering various domains and providing extensive detail about the metaphor's components. By utilizing this dataset, we are able to create a baseline model that sets a new standard in performance for visual metaphor interpretation. We believe that MetaCLUE will accelerate research into the automatic interpretation of visual metaphors, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of this complex linguistic phenomenon. Recent studies have found that human reading times do not align with the predictiveness of the context as measured by various large language models. This discrepancy raises questions about the limitations of current language models and the representational accuracy of human readers. To address this, researchers investigated the relationship between human reading times and predictiveness in two large language models, as well as in human readers. They analyzed the predictiveness of human readers by comparing their sentence completion responses to those of the models. The results showed that while human read times are closely linked to predictiveness, large language models fail to capture this relationship. This discrepancy may be due to the models' over-reliance on memorized information and their limited comprehension of human-like syntax. Ultimately, these findings highlight the need for more advanced models that better replicate human language processing strategies. Brain tumor segmentation from MRI data is a critical initial step in treatment planning.  MRI data, comprising T1, T1C, and T2 scans, is used to segment three distinct regions: tumor edema, the tumor core, and the necrotic area.  Traditional approaches rely solely on the MRI data itself, neglecting the fact that each image is associated with a patient's clinical history.  A novel 3D UNet architecture has been developed to address this issue by incorporating each patient's relevant clinical information as contextual data.  This approach effectively leverages clinical knowledge to enhance model performance, as demonstrated by experiments conducted on the BraTS 2018 dataset.  Moreover, the proposed model has been optimized to achieve greater efficiency and accuracy through the implementation of techniques such as batch normalization, drop-out, and multi-resolution training.  The model's effectiveness is evaluated using the Dice coefficient and average Hausdorff distance metrics.  A comprehensive analysis of the model's performance reveals its ability to accurately segment brain tumors and outperform existing methods.  The accompanying code for the proposed model is available for public access on the GitHub repository.  The code is designed to facilitate further research and improve the model's performance. Next, we apply and evaluate several state-of-the-art image object-detection models, including the use of different pre-trained visual representations and data augmentation methods. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset consisting of 2300 real-world historical maps and provide a performance comparison of our models on this and other established document image datasets. Through our experiments, we identify the optimal model architectures and training methods for effectively detecting document objects and discuss the implications of our findings. Moreover, we examine the effectiveness of using self-supervised learning and multi-task approaches to enhance object-detection performance. This study ultimately contributes a collection of new datasets, detailed performance evaluations, and practical recommendations for detecting document objects. The provided datasets are available at https://github.com/alefessmann/di_object_detection. The rise of the era of artificial intelligence has led to significant interest in the protection of intellectual property through copyright laws, resulting in the creation of various schemes to safeguard copyrights. Unfortunately, existing methods for dataset copyright protection have a major weakness as they necessitate additional hardware or easily detectable signals during training. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative dataset copyright protection approach through the incorporation of an advanced water marking technique. Our proposed system is capable of marking datasets with inoffensive and covert signals, which can then be used to assert ownership and prevent misuse. By leveraging a unique type of backdoor water marking that does not require specific triggers, we have developed a robust and efficient method for dataset protection. Our approach is evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K datasets, which have been marked with invisible patterns using a CNN model. Our results demonstrate the potential of this novel technique to safeguard against copyright infringement without compromising model performance. Moreover, the stealthy nature of this method makes it difficult to detect even when sophisticated tools are used to reverse-engineer the dataset. This work represents a pioneering effort in the dataset copyright protection domain by introducing a new watermarking technique that is both innocuous and covert. Our approach is expected to serve as a foundation for future research on the protection of intellectual property through dataset watermarking. Our code will be made available upon publication. Recent advancements in abstractive summarization models have demonstrated
superior performance over their non-neural counterparts. Nevertheless, these
models often produce fabricated information in their generated summaries.
To address this issue, researchers have proposed fact-aware summarization as
a viable solution, which aims to incorporate essential facts from source
documents into generated summaries. However, existing fact-aware summarization
models are limited in their ability to replicate original text from source
documents. Consequently, they tend to stick to their generated summaries
instead of accurately summarizing the content. To address this limitation,
this paper introduces Loyal to the Original: Fact-Aware Abstractive
Summmarization (LOTOFA), which combines fact-aware summarization with
abstractive models. By doing so, generated summaries are forced to accurately
mirror the content in the source documents. To achieve this, LOTOFA employs a
novel fact-aware decoder that identifies and identifies essential facts from
source documents and generates text that is consistent with these facts. To
further enhance the model's performance, a novel semantic consistency loss
function is introduced to ensure that generated summaries align semantically
with source document content. Through rigorous evaluation on two benchmark
datasets, LOTOFA outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of
producing accurate and coherent summaries that accurately reflect source
document content. Furthermore, LOTOFA's results demonstrate significant

This paper introduces a collection of tools designed for analyzing continuous gravitational waves by incorporating them into Octave code. Continuous gravitational waves pose a significant challenge in astrophysics due to the difficulty in pinpointing the source's location and its oscillatory nature. To facilitate further research in this field, we compiled a collection of tools written in Octave that can be utilized to develop and test methods for identifying continuous gravitational waves, particularly those orbiting compact objects in binary systems. These tools provide functionality for generating synthetic data, fitting models to real data, and searching for hiccups using the frequency-domain representation of gravitational waves, among other things. As an example of their utility, we applied the signal estimation code to identify the gravitational wave emission from GK Basliyan, a known pulsar in a binary system. We found the resulting signal to be consistent with noise, indicating that it may have been too faint to detect through standard methods. Neural machine translation systems struggle to process long sequences due to their reliance on global training objectives, which can lead to an exponential increase in required memory and computational power. To address this limitation, we have developed a sequence-to-sequence model that incorporates cross-modal alignment for neural machine translation systems with restricted resources. Our proposed model utilizes a target language model that is trained on the fly and can generate translations in real-time, leveraging the encoder and encoder's attention maps to determine which parts of the input are relevant and should be included in the translation. Our experiments demonstrate that this model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark datasets across multiple language pairs. Additionally, we have found that this model can successfully translate long input sequences with high efficiency, using significantly less memory and processing power than traditional neural machine translation systems. Our model's real-time translation capability also enables it to process input in real-time, even when the sequence is incomplete. This makes it an ideal candidate for use in real-time translation applications such as voice translation. Our proposed model's ability to translate effectively with significantly less memory and processing resources also makes it an attractive solution for use in low-resource translation settings. To achieve this, we utilize the BCS-BEC model to generate equations of state, considering both attractive and repulsive interactions. By employing a variational many-body approach, we calculate the mass-radius relationships for these models at a temperature of 0.1 MeV. Notably, our findings indicate that the maximum mass for the BEC model is approximately 2.2 solar masses, while its radius is roughly 10 km, with the temperature effect contributing a mass reduction of about 0.1 solar mass and a radius reduction of 1 km. Furthermore, we also examine the effects of pressure and chemical potential, as well as the surface tension and compactness of these strange stars. Our analysis, based on a nonlinear coupling of electron-phonon and optical-phonon-phonon interactions, shows that the damage process can be attributed to the nonlinear generation of optical-phonon modes, triggered by the initial heat induced by electron heating. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the nonlinearity arises from the modulation of optical-phonon modes by thermal expansion, driven by the phonon population. Our simulations reveal that the damage process can be understood by examining the evolution of the optical-phonon population, and we identify two distinct regimes of laser intensity: a non-damage regime characterized by a smooth increase in intensity, and a damage regime marked by a sudden threshold intensity above which the laser induces nonlinear optical-phonon generation and material damage. Our analysis, supported by experimental data, provides a microscopic understanding of the damage process in silicon and sheds light on the role of nonlinearity in laser-material interactions. GANs have become increasingly popular for their ability to generate complex image data. Despite their potential, GAN training can be challenging due to mode collapse, which occurs when the generator produces very few output samples despite its potential for many. Previous research has attempted to address mode collapse through various techniques, but there has been a lack of in-depth investigation into the underlying reasons and effects of these methods. This study investigates mode collapse in GAN training by analyzing Hessian eigenvalues during backpropagation, identifying a correlation between Hessian spectral radius and mode collapse. We also introduce a new approach, "Hessian-aware learning rate decay", which dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on Hessian eigenvalues, leading to improved mode diversity and performance. Our experiments on three datasets and two architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the Hessian spectrum and learning rate decay process. In manufacturing defect detection, hyperspectral imaging is a significant and growing field. To achieve high detection rates and minimize costs, defect detection systems often employ optimized scanning patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach to designing progressive hexagonal grids for hyperspectral imaging systems. By interweaving two hexagonal patterns, we create an efficient scanning pattern with uniform capture of spectral and spatial data, outperforming circular scanning methods. The proposed method enables reduced scan times while maintaining high detection rates, making it suitable for real-time defect detection applications. The methodology is composed of three key steps: designing individual hexagonal grids, determining the interweaving ratio, and identifying the optimal starting point. The proposed method is exemplified through its application to a practical hyperspectral imaging scenario. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed method in real-world hyperspectral imaging systems. Future wireless communication networks will heavily rely on Cloud Radio Access Networks (C-RANs), which enable the centralized processing of user data through a virtual node called the Virtual Cell. However, this approach may limit cell coverage in scenarios where the Base Station is far from users due to its cell being defined by a fixed area. To address this issue, we propose a set-theoretic learning method for cell coverage optimization in cell-less C-RANs. This method involves designing a cell expansion strategy that considers the optimal receive power threshold for each user, allowing the BS to adjust its beamforming vectors and receive power levels to ensure coverage for all users within the expanded cell. This process involves solving a complex optimization problem that accounts for power consumption and user rate requirements. To simplify this problem, we propose a two-stage optimization method that first solves a convex problem to obtain a feasible power threshold, and then uses a non-convex optimization technique to find the optimal beamforming vectors. Additionally, a low-complexity approach based on clustering is proposed to further reduce computational complexity. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of power consumption, with a significant improvement in user rates. Moreover, the results show that the proposed low-complexity approach achieves comparable performance while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements. This set-theoretic learning method can be further extended to optimize cell expansion in multi-cell C-RAN systems. To this end, we propose a method for expanding multiple cells simultaneously, which involves solving a non-convex joint optimization problem to obtain a power allocation for all users within the expanded cells. This problem is reformulated as a complex convex optimization problem, which is solved using a joint optimization technique. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method. This research paper outlines a method for detecting and resolving conflicts in complex process descriptions. Key contributions include a systematic approach for managing conflicts that can be applied to various description languages and a specific technique for enforcing one-outline semantics in hybrid processes. The proposed method can be used to derive unique, equivalent process descriptions with reduced complexity. Furthermore, it enables the transformation of an arbitrary hybrid process into its most simplified, one-outline form. Additionally, we introduce a new semantics for describing processes that incorporate an initial, terminal state. Deep Q-learning algorithms, specifically ensemble Q-learning, have been widely adopted for their effectiveness in balancing performance and stability. Despite their success, these algorithms are susceptible to a critical issue - the value function collapsing problem. This issue arises when multiple individual Q-functions converge to a single solution, resulting in poor generalization capabilities. To prevent this issue, we developed a novel regularization technique. By applying a divergent-promoting objective, we can ensure maximum diversity in the representation of individual Q-functions. Experimental evaluations on various datasets confirmed the superiority of our approach in preventing the value function collapse. Notably, ensemble Q-learning with our regularization outperformed other algorithms, even when data was limited. Moreover, regularized ensemble Q-learning demonstrated more stable learning and better value function generalization than other algorithms, making it a promising choice for reinforcement learning tasks. Notably, this algorithm achieved a groundbreaking mean return of 1023.7 on the atari breaking blocks game, even when using only 100 episodes. This is a significant milestone, even for the top-performing algorithms, which typically require millions of episodes to succeed. Our findings suggest that maximizing representation diversity in ensemble Q-learning with our regularization technique can lead to improved generalization capabilities and robustness to unseen situations, a crucial aspect in real-world applications. This breakthrough opens up new avenues for research, enabling the development of more effective reinforcement learning algorithms that can handle complex, dynamic environments with ease. With our regularization technique, researchers can now create more robust reinforcement learning agents, even in the presence of noisy data or changing environments. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the field of reinforcement learning, enabling agents to learn more efficiently and generalize better in a wide range of applications. This novel method is versatile and can be applied to a range of celestial bodies, offering a streamlined alternative to established methods with the added benefit of reduced computational requirements. When compared to established methods, our approach exhibits a relatively small error margin of 0.0012% for Mercury and 0.0015% for Venus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach produces more accurate results than the Euler method, which yielded an error margin of 0.0035% for Mercury and 0.0044% for Venus. To further validate our approach, we also precomputed precession periods for a range of celestial bodies, including Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus over a period of 50,000 years, with the results showing a high degree of consistency with established data. Researchers examined how these resonant modes, influenced by the Earth's harmonics, affect the ionospheric plasma and propagate with extremely low damping. Owing to their weak dissipation, these modes can persist for hours, extending their spatial reach. As a result, they may interact with the ionized plasma in the lower atmosphere, particularly in the ionospheric regions, and alter the density of free electrons. This altered electron density can, in turn, influence the Earth's magnetic field intensity. Since the human body is composed of ionized fluids like the brain, researchers investigated the possibility of resonant modes interacting with these biological components. Using a mathematical model, they calculated the effect of resonant modes on the electron density within the brain and the resulting changes in the magnetic field. Notably, the brain's magnetic field fluctuations could be detectable with a SQUID sensor, allowing for a potentially viable experimental setup. However, the estimated changes in the brain's magnetic field are relatively small, approximately $0.1 pT$ for the Earth's harmonics at $3d$, which might be below the resolution of some SQUID sensors. Researchers also considered the possibility of using artificial magnetic fields to manipulate the human body's magnetic properties. This investigation was based on a simplified model of the brain as a spherical capacitor, which enabled them to estimate the changes in the electron density and the magnetic field intensity. Notably, the estimated changes in the electron density might be measurable with modern techniques like functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). This research provides a theoretical foundation for an experimental setup that could explore the impact of resonant ionospheric modes on the human body's biological properties. Nonetheless, the study's findings are purely theoretical and not supported by empirical evidence. Consequently, the results should be viewed as hypothetical until experimental evidence is obtained to confirm the existence of such an interaction. However, this relationship is distinct when comparing the compact crystal configuration to a more extended plasma surrounding a smaller, isolated ion. In this case, the crystal's temperature is inversely related to its size and directly related to the average plasma density. The long-standing challenge of guaranteeing secure, confidential communication over networks has been partially addressed by various protocols, yet a fundamental issue persists. Conventional key-exchange protocols, which are often employed in conjunction with others like TLS and rely on assumptions about the adversary, have limitations, particularly in terms of perfect security and resistance to certain attacks. To address this, we introduce Wink, a novel key-exchange protocol that ensures secure, confidential communication and leverages existing infrastructure to provide robust security guarantees. By capitalizing on network performance features such as packet loss and NTP drift, Wink enables key exchange without relying on key centers, offering an alternative to existing protocols like TLS. Furthermore, Wink's design is flexible and adaptable to various network conditions, including those with limited network connectivity. To evaluate its effectiveness, we implemented Wink and conducted a series of experiments, demonstrating its potential for practical and resilient key exchange in scenarios where traditional protocols may be insufficient. Overall, Wink offers a more straightforward and efficient approach to secure communication that outperforms existing protocols in certain challenging environments. The Riemannian radiative transfer equation has gained significant attention in the fields of optics, spectroscopy, and astrophysics due to its extensive applications. Inverse problems derived from this equation have far-reaching implications, and one such issue is determining scattering coefficients from measured intensity data under varying spectral conditions. In this context, we explore the influence of temperature fluctuations on coefficient identification within a curved geometric framework. To address this challenge, we employ a novel convexification method, which involves formulating an optimization problem to minimize the discrepancy between calculated and observed intensity data. This approach is supported by numerical simulations conducted on the sphere, which demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying scattering coefficients in complex inverse problems, particularly in cases where non-linear relationships between data and coefficients are present. Notably, our results indicate that optimal solutions obtained through this method can serve as a reliable starting point for iterative optimization algorithms, thereby facilitating more efficient and accurate solutions to inverse coefficient problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of this method to a range of scenarios, including the analysis of cosmic dust and its potential for identifying atmospheric constituents in exoplanetary systems. Future research directions and potential applications of this approach are also discussed. The numerical simulations presented in this study utilize the Gummel algorithm, which is a global optimization method capable of handling non-linear problems. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and accompanying datasets are made available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/keivanfarhang/gummel.git. Vector algebra has been widely utilized in computer graphics for its efficiency in processing vectorial data, but it is hindered by the prevalence of sparse matrices in various applications. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed techniques to convert sparse matrix operations into vectorial operations, which are more computationally efficient. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages trace analysis to optimize sparse matrix conversions, enabling the creation of more efficient vectorial code by identifying and exploiting the dependencies inherent in the matrix operations. The trace analysis method is composed of two distinct phases: dependency analysis and trace merging. In dependency analysis, the researchers examine the relationships between the operations within a sparse matrix, resulting in a structured representation that preserves the order of the operations. This phase is followed by trace merging, where the researchers combine the dependencies of the resulting traces to optimize their efficiency. This approach is particularly useful in fields such as physics-based animation, where complex sparse matrices arise from integrating physics engines with rendering engines. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, the researchers applied it to a variety of sparse matrices derived from real-world scenarios, including sparse matrix multiplications and transformations, and matrix exponentials, resulting in improved performance by up to 5x compared to existing vectorial conversions. The implementation of this method is publicly available on GitHub. In addition, the researchers provide a set of tools for automatically converting sparse matrix code into more efficient vectorial code, which can be applied to a range of applications. It is found that the dilaton's non-trivial role extends beyond mere adjustment of kinetic terms and constant vacuum energy, instead introducing dynamic interactions between these elements. Notably, the phenomenon known as "double dilaton dynamics" arises when both the dilaton and dilatons (the two components of the B-field) play an active role in the dynamics. This results in the dilaton modifying the relationship between these entities and the cosmological constant, giving rise to a dynamic interaction between them. Moreover, the analysis reveals that the conventional understanding of constant vacuum energy is insufficient for describing the dynamics of cosmological constants supported by non-constant kinetic terms. This is demonstrated by the observation that the transition from kinetic dominance to constant vacuum energy is continuous rather than discontinuous. As a consequence, the conventional hierarchy between the cosmological constant and kinetic energy is not a strict one, and the dynamics of cosmological constants can exhibit significant nonlinearity. These findings are expected to have significant implications for theories attempting to explain the low value of the cosmological constant. They may also shed light on the mechanism by which the cosmological constant is driven to a constant value during inflation. Additionally, the analysis suggests that the dynamics of the dilaton could be a key factor in explaining the observed smallness of the cosmological constant. This is achieved through the investigation of the cosmological implications of the non-trivial properties of the dilaton. Specifically, the analysis reveals that the transition from kinetic dominance to constant vacuum energy is characterized by a continuous change in the value of the dilaton. This, in turn, gives rise to a non-trivial relationship between the cosmological constant and kinetic energy. This complex relationship is expected to have significant implications for our understanding of the low value of the cosmological constant. We derive the thermodynamic characteristics of causal diamonds in both unaccelerated and accelerated $AdS_2$ and $dS_2$ spacetimes. The causal diamonds are generated by causal embeddings of Minkowski space into these spacetimes. The analysis reveals that the thermodynamic energy of causal diamonds in both dS and AdS backgrounds is finite and non-zero, whereas their entropy remains zero. Furthermore, an accelerated Causal Diamond in dS$_2$ generates an observer-dependent, linearly accelerated thermal radiation bath, and the temperature of this radiation experienced by the embedding observer is found to be constant. High-energy physics data analysis heavily relies on data merging, which is crucial for current and future experiments. As data rates surge, parallel processing in data storage is essential to facilitate real-time analysis. This research focuses on merging data within a single file using the HDF5 format, and introduces a novel, parallel merging approach that leverages multi-threading. This innovative technique boasts substantial performance gains over existing parallel merging techniques. This article details a real-world application of this parallel merging method, which was employed in the analysis of data from the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Specifically, it was used in the simulation reconstruction of Z+jet events, which required merging large datasets into a single, comprehensive dataset. This merged dataset enabled researchers to accurately replicate Z+jet events, and ultimately contributed to the analysis of Z+jet events in the context of Higgs boson research. This research demonstrates the importance of parallel merging in facilitating data analysis, and highlights its potential benefits in high-energy physics research. Furthermore, our results show that the parallel merging approach used in this study outperforms existing methods by significantly reducing processing time, and demonstrating enhanced scalability on multi-core systems. By reducing processing time by 40% and increasing scalability by 6.5x, our results demonstrate the superiority of this novel parallel merging technique. By releasing the code behind this study, we aim to empower researchers in high-energy physics to harness the power of parallel processing and enhance their data analysis capabilities. Our code is freely available, and can be accessed at https://github.com/ATLAS-HEP-Collaboration/ParallelMerge. We believe that this research has the potential to revolutionize data merging practices within the high-energy physics research community. Our research findings are available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.13230. Additionally, our code has been released under the GNU General Public License v3.0, and is available for use by the scientific community. A variant of automata theory known as pushdown timed automata (PTA) combines features of stochastic and deterministic models, allowing it to model both continuous and discrete behaviors. Researchers have developed algorithms to determine the reachability of specific states in a PTA, with some achieving a high degree of efficiency (efficiency class PSPACE). Building upon this work, our paper introduces three new algorithms for PTA reachability that operate within specific subspaces of PTA configurations, each offering a unique advantage in terms of computational speed. By leveraging a zone-based approach, we demonstrate that these algorithms can achieve a speedup over existing solutions, with a speed of 1/4 for certain conditions, 1/10 for others, and a speedup of a constant factor for a third condition. Image dehazing is a critical image processing task that affects visual perception and has numerous real-world applications. Existing dehazing methods can be categorized into two approaches: direct image reconstruction and image refocusing, but they often struggle to achieve optimal results due to their limitations. This paper presents a novel image dehazing method, called the Feature Affinity Learning Network (FALN), which leverages a unique feature affinity learning mechanism to extract high-quality image features from both clear images and hazy images. By employing an attention module to learn and mimic the way the human visual system perceives and compares features, FALN generates feature affinity maps that represent the similarities between different feature channels. This feature affinity information is then used to guide the learning of rich, high-quality image features in a subsequent module. At the output stage, FALN uses a feature fusion module to integrate the learned features from both clear images and hazy images and produces high-quality, dehazed images. Experimental results demonstrate that FALN outperforms existing dehazing methods in terms of both subjective and objective evaluations. Furthermore, FALN is computationally efficient and can be implemented in a modular and scalable framework that can be easily adapted to other image processing tasks. Voice conversion, a technique for transforming one voice into another, has been an area of focus in speech research. Recent advancements in diffusion-based generative models have led to notable breakthroughs in voice conversion. In this paper, a new voice conversion framework called DiffSVC is presented, utilizing a denoising diffusion framework with a novel training method that combines a target speaker's voice with a source speaker's original voice to create a more authentic conversion process. An efficient algorithm is also proposed to accelerate the conversion process, which significantly outperforms existing models in voice conversion quality. Experiments demonstrate that DiffSVC produces natural-sounding speech with the desired voice and achieves state-of-the-art performance in voice conversion. Moreover, the model's training efficiency results in a faster conversion process with superior quality compared to existing approaches. Specifically, we examine the connection between the Gibbs measures driven by various external field configurations. To achieve this, we establish a framework of diamond operators, which allows us to derive a rigorous bound on the discrepancy between the two measures. Our method is founded on a novel combinatorial analysis that leverages hypergraph theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our approach can be generalized to a broader class of models, including those with nearest-neighbor interactions defined through generic potentials. Additionally, we provide an extension of our results to a specific class of models, which includes an approximation of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Moreover, we derive an expression for the replica number in the context of the SK model, which aligns with the Parisi solution. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can be used to establish a variational principle for the free energy density of the Ising model, which is parameterized by different external fields. This principle is analogous to the principle of maximum entropy, but with a different action functional. Finally, we discuss potential future directions and research paths. Few-shot learning, a problem of limited labeled data, poses a significant challenge 
in our world, where many problems are hard to annotate due to their complexity. 
This paper proposes a new solution, Meta-filtering, which enhances existing few-shot 
learning meta-learning methods. By integrating a filter module, Meta-filtering improves 
the accuracy of meta-learning methods, particularly under class-imbalance conditions. 
The filter module adjusts sample weights via a dynamic filter to rectify class-imbalance 
issues and, further, corrects sample biases to boost the accuracy of meta-learning methods. 
Experiments on three few-shot image recognition datasets confirm the effectiveness of Meta-filtering.

Our work is the first to use a filter module to enhance meta-learning methods for few-shot learning. 
Our method is also the first to use a dynamic filter module to adjust sample weights for improved accuracy.

In the field of medical imaging, the challenge of domain shift significantly hampers the generalization of deep learning models trained on abundant data sources to a limited number of target domains. To overcome this hurdle, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation approach that leverages domain-invariant features, graph-based convolutional networks, and pseudo-labeling to bridge the gap between source and target domains. By employing domain-invariant features, we achieve disentanglement through an autoencoder network and ensure that the extracted features are common across domains. Yet, existing literature neglects the fact that Tangle 2.0's consensus path can be subject to the 'last-payload problem,' where multiple nodes can generate new tips with equal legitimacy. To address this gap, we introduce a formal definition of the consensus path and demonstrate its potential for conflicts within Tangle 2.0. Additionally, we outline 'last-payload problem' scenarios and evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed solution in resolving them. Overall, our work clarifies the underlying mechanisms of Tangle 2.0 and highlights opportunities for improvement by building upon existing protocols. By shedding light on the strengths and limitations of Tangle 2.0, we aim to facilitate collaboration among researchers and developers to further advance this promising blockchain protocol. Recent advancements in transformer-based semantic segmentation models have achieved
impressive performance, yet they often come with the drawbacks of high computational
cost, low efficiency, and prolonged inference times, particularly on resource-limited
mobile devices. To address this challenge, we introduce RTFormer, a cutting-edge
semantic segmentation model that leverages a novel transformer architecture and
efficient multi-head self-attention learning. By incorporating a novel attention mask
and a reduced self-attention network, RTFormer offers accelerated processing and
optimized performance. Our experiments demonstrate that RTFormer surpasses its
competitors in efficiency, achieving notable improvements in inference speed and
mated performance on the CamVid and ADE20K datasets. Furthermore, RTFormer's
state-of-the-art performance on these platforms validates its superiority over
existing models, both in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Our source code
is available for public access on GitHub at https://github.com/taohuang1994/RTFormer.

The impact of geographical factors on earthquake occurrence is a significant consideration in seismology, but studying this influence is complex due to the necessity for models that can capture both the spatial patterns of earthquake densities and the underlying temporal processes of individual events. This study develops an approach to analyze the effects of geographical variables on earthquake occurrence by integrating a spatially varying Cox process model with a nonhomogeneous, piecewise exponential intensity model. By employing a Markovian Gaussian field, we develop a model that can accommodate varying earthquake rates over time and space. Through simulation-based inference using a particle optimization algorithm, we apply this approach to data from the Japanese earthquake dataset and examine how different geographical factors, including the distance from the ocean and major faults, influence earthquake occurrence. Our results demonstrate the potential of this method for quantifying the relationships between geographical variables and earthquake occurrence patterns. This approach can be used to analyze the effects of geographical factors on a wide range of spatio-temporal point processes. By integrating our method with machine learning techniques, we can develop more accurate models of earthquake occurrence. This research provides a foundation for future studies on the role of geographical factors in earthquake occurrence. Our method involves assigning fractional amounts of traffic to each path, ensuring that the total amount of traffic through each node remains proportional to its degree. This is a natural extension of existing network trimming methods, which assign traffic in whole units. We've created a simple algorithm to implement this approach by repeatedly adjusting path weights and node proportions until convergence. Our simulations show that network trimming via resource redistribution outperforms existing methods, particularly for 100-Gb/s networks, often by a significant margin. This approach also results in more balanced traffic patterns, which can be advantageous for other network management techniques. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our method can be implemented in conjunction with existing network trimming techniques, leading to an even more effective state planning solution. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of considering fractional traffic assignments in network management and suggest that network trimming via resource redistribution is a valuable addition to the existing toolkit. Future research directions involve exploring the application of our method to other areas of network management. Language models can utilize pre-trained ASR representations to enhance their language understanding and generation capabilities. By fine-tuning a language model on ASR representations, it can learn to generate text conditioned on the predicted labels of an ASR. This approach allows LM access to the entire vocabulary of the ASR, potentially expanding text generation capabilities to any language. In this study, we examine the LM training process and its ability to generate text conditioned on ASR labels for approximately 2000 languages, leveraging a large ASR dataset. We also investigate the effectiveness of LM fine-tuning and its relationship with the ASR training data size. Our results demonstrate that LM can successfully generate text for previously unseen languages during inference by predicting them, and we achieve notable gains in perplexity and translation metrics when applying this technique to the "Can You Understand Me Then?" challenge. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the LM's perplexity is influenced by the ASR training data size. Consequently, we propose that the ASR training data size could serve as a proxy to measure the quality of the ASR model for languages. This research has been accepted for publication in ICML 2022. Additionally, we have developed a Python library called asr2k that enables language generation capabilities for any language. This library can be accessed via the repository at https://github.com/allenai/asr2k. A video presentation of the study can be found at https://youtu.be/6s5qzqzqzqz. A patient's symptoms, lifestyle, and medical history often provide the most valuable information for healthcare professionals to make accurate diagnoses.  However, patients frequently struggle to effectively convey their symptoms, leading to misinterpretation by healthcare providers.  To address this issue, our research introduces a new multimodal conversational model, known as InsightGC, designed to help patients convey their symptoms more clearly and enable healthcare professionals to make more informed diagnoses.  By integrating a graph memory network with a conversational model, InsightGC effectively captures a patient's clinical context, ultimately enhancing symptom detection and analysis.  Through extensive experiments on a large dataset, our research demonstrates the superior performance of InsightGC in detecting and extracting key symptoms, outperforming existing models by 7-12% in end-to-end tasks and 4-5% in symptom extraction tasks, respectively.  Furthermore, our results show that InsightGC improves the accuracy of clinical decision-making, leading to a 2-4% increase in the quality of diagnoses.  To facilitate future research, we have made our dataset and model publicly available.  By empowering patients to convey their symptoms more effectively and empowering healthcare professionals with more comprehensive clinical data, our work has the potential to improve patient-physician interactions, diagnoses, and treatment plans, leading to better patient outcomes. Furthermore, our results suggest that multimodal conversational models like InsightGC could be valuable in remote healthcare settings. The results indicate that the phase correlation can be categorized into three types: destructive, correlated, and destructive-correlated. However, when the transmitter and receiver are in motion, their relative phase correlation becomes correlated, which can be harnessed to improve detection performance. In the realm of active learning, researchers have been investigating how to minimize the requirement for labeled data by selectively sampling it. Active learning algorithms typically aim to choose unlabeled samples that can most benefit the model trained on labeled data. However, this approach has a limitation - it assumes that the model will perform better with more labeled data. This is not always the case, and we have observed instances where the model may worsen with additional labeled data. This paper presents a new perspective on active learning, where the focus is on improving the model's test performance. Based on this criterion, we have devised a new sampling strategy that chooses the sample that will yield the highest enhancement in test performance. Our approach is model-agnostic, requiring only one pass through the dataset to identify such samples. Through experiments on various tasks, we have found that this strategy outperforms several other active learning methods. When we also consider the cost of labeling, our strategy is competitive with the most effective approaches. Our findings suggest that enhancing test performance is a viable alternative objective for active learning, and we have made our code available. Our work aims to bridge the gap between film studies and machine learning, opening up new avenues for empirical research. To better understand human physical abilities and improve overall health, researchers have been analyzing physiological signals, including heart rate. However, measuring heart rate manually can be time-consuming and impractical, making automated analysis crucial. Recent approaches using camera-based assessments have shown promise, but there are still challenges to be addressed, particularly when it comes to intense exercise. We have developed a new method that leverages video data to estimate heart rate even during high-intensity activities like running and cycling. The approach involves a two-part system: first, it uses facial recognition to identify key features and calculates heart rate data from these points; then, it employs a deep learning model to refine this information and provide accurate heart rate predictions. This system has been tested on videos of individuals engaged in intense exercise and found to outperform previous methods, demonstrating a correlation coefficient of 0.967 when compared to manually recorded heart rate data. The approach also yields promising results when applied to less intense exercise like rowing and triathlon events where heart rate data is automatically synchronized with the physical activity. The method's effectiveness is further highlighted by its ability to be applied to videos of individuals performing high-intensity interval training, a scenario where previous methods failed to deliver reliable results. The code for this analysis will be made publicly available. The findings of this study are significant and have potential implications for the development of future wearable devices that can automatically track physical activity and heart rate. The research has far-reaching implications and could potentially be used to assess physical abilities and identify individuals at risk of cardiovascular diseases. Comprising an enhanced forwarding mechanism and intelligent end-to-end algorithm, Absorber operates efficiently at both network core and user levels, scales linearly, and supports zero-traffic-latency forwarding of uniform-sized data. When integrated with standard transport protocols, Absorber enables reliable, high-throughput, and low-latency connections for a wide range of applications, including those with dynamic bandwidth requirements. Through comprehensive simulations, we have validated the performance of Absorber under various scenarios and network configurations. This solution has been successfully implemented and tested on a real-world network, yielding impressive results. Notably, Absorber supports flexible configurations, including dynamic mappings, which enable flexible forwarding at both network core and user levels, thereby enhancing the solution's adaptability and effectiveness. As a result, Absorber offers significant advantages over traditional forwarding protocols, particularly in terms of its ability to achieve predictable delivery of packets. for securing transactions and communications in various sectors such as finance 
and identity verification. To advance this concept, we have developed a set 
of fundamental principles that outline the key requirements for any quantum 
proof system. Building on these principles, we have created a universal method 
for generating authentic quantum certificates. This method, which we call 
quantization, allows any classical proof to be transformed into a quantum 
equivalent while maintaining its original meaning. Through this process, we 
have demonstrated that quantum certificates possess multiple benefits over their 
classical counterparts, including guaranteed security against hacking, 
efficient verification, and the ability to be publicly shared without 
compromising confidentiality. Our findings provide a solid foundation for 
further exploring the potential of quantum certificates in various 
applications, and they may inspire new ideas in the field of quantum 
informatics. To facilitate future advancements, we have made our research 
results available in two open-source repositories on GitHub. The first 
repository contains a framework for generating quantum certificates, and the 
second repository features a prototype of the quantum blockchain platform, 
ChainiQ, which incorporates the quantum certificate system. This platform 
includes tools for creating, verifying, and communicating in quantum 
networks, and it provides a foundation for developing quantum-based 
blockchain systems. With ChainiQ, users can create and verify quantum-based 
smart contracts, certificates, and other types of quantum documents. To 
demonstrate the feasibility of our approach, we have successfully deployed a 
quantum blockchain on a cloud-based platform, and we have achieved a 
quantum signature in just 0.11 milliseconds with a 99.9% success rate. This 
quantum signature has been stored in a blockchain system, and it can be 
verified in a few milliseconds. Our research has opened up new possibilities 
for quantum technology, and we believe that it will drive the development of 
quantum infrastructure, paving the way for a new generation of quantum 
technologies. The future of this field is full of promise, and we are eager to

Recent breakthroughs in NLP have led to the development of advanced language representations, primarily through the use of large, multilingual language models. However, the impact of language typology on these models remains poorly understood. This paper aims to address this gap by examining the influence of language typological characteristics on language representations using the Uralic family of languages. Our findings show that language typology is linked to linguistic similarity and can be used to explain model performance in zero-shot learning tasks. Furthermore, we observed that language representations are affected by typological characteristics such as isolating language features, with isolating languages exhibiting stronger representations, and notable differences exist among Uralic languages such as Finnish, Hungarian, and Sami. Our research also reveals that language representations are not solely defined by individual features, but rather by the interplay of language features, and language family relationships can be captured by a multilingual model trained on related languages. This paper provides new insights into the relationship between language representations and language typology. In reinforcement learning, reward functions play a pivotal role. However, reward specification can be a major challenge due to the common issue of sparse reward feedback. Researchers have developed various solutions to address this issue, categorized into two distinct approaches: one focusing on modifying the environment's dynamics to increase exploration, and the other, which takes a more direct approach by altering the reward function itself. In response, we propose a semantic-aware denoising approach that leverages the semantic representations of pre-trained language models to filter out unwanted semantic discrepancies between languages. By incorporating semantic similarity as a new evaluation criterion, our proposed method guides model training towards reducing semantic disparities without sacrificing the desired semantic structures in target translations. Through extensive experimentation on multiple benchmark datasets for English-to-German, English-to-French, and English-to-Czech translation tasks, our proposed method has been shown to surpass various baseline models in terms of both automatic and human evaluations. Most notably, our results demonstrate that semantic denoising enhances translation performance consistently across a wide range of model architectures and pre-training settings. Overall, our findings suggest that semantic denoising is a valuable strategy for mitigating the effects of semantic disparities in pre-trained language models for Neural Machine Translation. We introduce a novel approach called adversarial learned fair representations using mitigation and stacking, denoted as ALFR-MS, to create unbiased data representations in the absence of sensitive attribute information. This method consists of two stages: mitigation and adjustment. The mitigation stage removes biases from data and the adjustment stage fine-tunes the representation to improve its quality. We evaluate our proposed approach, ALFR-MS, on four datasets and compare it to other fair representation learning methods. The experimental results demonstrate that ALFR-MS achieves superior performance in learning fair representations across different datasets. The source code for our approach is available on a public platform.

This research paper explores load balancing models in heterogeneous parallel systems where arrival rates and service times are dynamic, specified by Markovian Arrival Processes and Phase-Type distributions, respectively. Load balancing is achieved through a state-dependent random migration policy that minimizes average system length. The primary goal is to calculate an optimal random policy that minimizes system response times, which can be an impractical task due to the complex nature of MARAP+PH models. To overcome this challenge, we employ a doubly exponential approach, which involves constructing a large-scale finite-state space Markov chain to approximate the response time distribution. By leveraging the properties of PH distributions, we simplify the analysis and derive an efficient algorithm for state grouping, which significantly reduces state space size. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical experiments and identify the performance limitations of load balancing models caused by the inherent randomness of the system. Additionally, we analyze the impact of parameter variations on the optimal policy performance and examine the trade-off between migration rate and response time under different system conditions. The results show that our approach is computationally efficient and provides a reliable approximation of response time distributions. Moreover, we find that the optimal policy is relatively insensitive to parameter changes and that migration rate has a negligible effect on response time performance. The findings of this research offer valuable insights into the behavior of load balancing models and provide guidance for designing optimal policies that are robust to parameter variations in MARAP+PH models. The research also serves as a foundation for future studies on load balancing models with more complex arrival and service processes. The analysis of JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) metrics is becoming increasingly important due to its widespread use. Despite this, there is a lack of comprehensive JSON metrics research, particularly when it comes to comparing them to traditional relational data base schema metrics. Building on the work of Lohr-Kropaa, who proposed a framework for evaluating JSON document structure, we aim to advance the state of the art. We start by identifying relevant JSON metrics, which are then refined through a multi-objective optimization process. The resulting set of 14 metrics is employed to analyze large JSON documents, with an emphasis on identifying potential security risks, such as SQL injection vulnerabilities. Additionally, we investigate the connection between our proposed metrics and common security-related metrics derived from relational data base schema. Furthermore, we conduct a case study to examine the effectiveness of our metrics in detecting potential security issues in JSON data sources. The JSON Metrics Analyzer (JMA) is a tool designed to automate the analysis of JSON metrics, making it easier to utilize our research in practical applications. The JMA tool is available under the terms of the MIT open-source software license, hosted on a publicly accessible GitHub repository. The associated dataset used in this study is also available through the U.S. Government Digital Analytics Program Open Data repository. As a supplementary resource, we provide a comprehensive appendix that offers additional insights and background information on JSON metrics, along with a deeper examination of the Lohr-Kropaa framework and its extension to multi-objective optimization. The appendix also includes a thorough analysis of the connection between our proposed metrics and traditional relational data base schema metrics, which has been overlooked in existing research. Ultimately, the goal of this research is to provide a solid foundation for future studies on JSON metrics, particularly when it comes to identifying potential security issues in JSON data sources. identify concurrency bugs across single-threaded and multi-threaded environments.

In computer vision, attribute-based representations are often restricted by their need for extensive, costly annotations. To overcome this limitation, a novel method is proposed to learn attribute representations using only a few labeled examples, and this method is shown to be effective in attribute discovery and classification tasks. It achieves this by creating a probabilistic attribute model that can generate data samples. By combining this model with a variational random attribute generator, the method can generate specific data variations controlled by individual attributes. To further enhance its performance, the method incorporates an attribute classification task to refine its representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method excels state-of-the-art approaches, providing improved results across various datasets. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis is conducted to demonstrate the method's ability to generalize to unseen data, and its effectiveness in attribute discovery and classification tasks is shown to be superior to existing approaches. To address the challenges of energy-efficient networks, we introduce Energy-Conscious Network Operator Search (ENOS), an innovative approach for optimizing network operator selection. ENOS leverages a hybrid accelerator combining digital and compute-in-memory architectures to minimize energy consumption during inference. ENOS uses a genetic algorithm to discover the most energy-efficient network operator by exploring the vast operator space, outperforming existing solutions and achieving an average 20% energy reduction across diverse image classification benchmarks. ENOS also demonstrates substantial energy savings in a real-world deployment for a medical AI application, yielding an 80% reduction in energy consumption. ENOS's adaptability extends to various deployment scenarios, including edge, cloud, and medical imaging environments. Moreover, ENOS's method for selecting operators can be applied to various computational tasks beyond neural networks. In comparison, traditional approaches that optimize network operator selection via gradient-based learning require significantly more resources and struggle with convergence, whereas ENOS achieves superior results with minimal computational resources. ENOS's success stems from its ability to incorporate both hardware and software constraints, enabling it to outperform other approaches. Overall, ENOS provides a comprehensive and efficient solution for optimizing network operator selection to reduce energy consumption in deep learning accelerators. To enhance the development of intelligent driving systems, driving situation generation from vehicle trajectories is crucial, yet current methods fall short due to a lack of consideration for explicit knowledge integration, resulting in generated scenarios that are semantically implausible. This paper proposes a novel framework, ADIT, which combines explicit knowledge with adversarial learning to create realistic driving scenarios. By utilizing a hierarchical knowledge representation, which includes vehicle states, traffic rules, and road topologies, ADIT is able to condition scenario generation and integrate explicit knowledge via knowledge-guided noise injection and constraint regularization. Furthermore, ADIT employs a dual adversarial loss function to evaluate the semantic coherence of generated scenarios in relation to the corresponding vehicle trajectories and road topologies. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of ADIT, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments, which also rely on vehicle states and road topologies. The problem of enhancing viewing graphs is a critical component in the development of visual simultaneous localization and mapping systems, particularly when dealing with partially observable environments. Existing methods for addressing this problem are often limited to a two-step process that first estimates the robot's position and orientation, and subsequently calculates the optimal viewing sequence. However, these approaches can be time-consuming and may not always yield the global optimal solution. In this study, we propose a novel formulation of the viewing graph enhancement problem that simultaneously determines the robot's position and orientation, as well as its optimal viewing sequence. By formulating this problem as a constrained integer programming problem, we demonstrate its ability to converge to a globally optimal solution in a reasonable amount of time. Additionally, our proposed solution exhibits robustness to various measurement noise and demonstrates its superiority over existing approaches through simulation results that highlight the significance of simultaneous optimization. The code underlying our proposed solution is publicly available on the 3DVL library. This contribution presents an innovative solution to a complex problem in the field of simultaneous localization and mapping, providing a more efficient and effective approach than existing methods for enhancing viewing graphs that can be applied to a wide range of applications. The results of our experiments show that our proposed solution significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art, with a 2-fold increase in loop closure detection rates and a 2.5-fold reduction in the number of required measurements. Moreover, our approach is capable of handling a wide variety of environments, including those with limited visibility, and can be easily adapted for use in various applications. The key contributions of this study are twofold: the development of a more efficient and effective approach to viewing graph enhancement that can be easily adapted for use in various applications, and the demonstration of a new formulation of the viewing graph enhancement problem that can be solved using a combination of mathematical formulations and numerical methods. This novel formulation has the potential to converge to a globally optimal solution, and our experiments show that it is capable of outperforming existing approaches in a wide range of applications. NapierOne stands out as one of the largest mixed file datasets available, offering research opportunities in near-duplicate detection, cross-format text extraction, and document metadata analysis. Notably, this dataset provides a contemporary perspective, featuring recent content, unlike existing datasets such as Govdocs1, which is based on older information. Our approach to designing spatial structures focuses on the implementation of
user-defined objectives through AI-assisted methods. To address this, we've
developed a novel framework that integrates reinforcement learning with self-play.
The system learns a spatial representation of a given objective function, where
agents construct components from a predefined set of shapes with specified sizes
and rotations. By applying this framework to the optimization of a periodic
microstructure with desired mechanical properties, we've demonstrated its ability
to identify efficient designs that meet the objective. Notably, our method
exhibits robustness to design imperfections and can be easily extended to tackle
a wide range of problems in material science and engineering. The system can
also be utilized to create novel structures that meet user-specified performance
criteria. Overall, our approach represents a significant breakthrough in spatial
construction techniques, enabling the identification of optimal designs that
satisfy user-defined objectives. The corresponding code is publicly available on
GitHub at the specified URL. The results of this study will be presented at an
upcoming conference. Additional findings will be shared in a future publication. 
We intend to further develop and refine this foundational work to address a
broader range of spatial problems in a future publication. The accompanying video
demonstrates the system's ability to learn designs that can withstand various
mechanical loads.

Monocular 3D object detection has become a significant challenge in the field of autonomous driving due to its importance in identifying objects using a single camera. The main hurdle to overcome in the development of autonomous vehicles is creating a reliable and accurate 3D object detection system. This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the performance of monocular 3D object detection by integrating depth information into the dynamic message transmission process. The depth information is utilized to condition the dynamic message transmission, enabling the transmission to better comprehend object depth and distance. The proposed method is straightforward to implement and computationally efficient, requiring no modifications to backbones or other components. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark, surpassing the previous best model by 2.4% and 0.2% in 3D mAP and 3D IOU metrics. In particular, the task of multi-label image classification benefits from substantial amounts of unlabeled data and data with a balanced label distribution.  We propose an approach that leverages a contrastive loss function to generate high-quality image representations, which we then utilize to train a baseline model that can handle multi-label classification with imbalanced labels.  We then develop a new method that combines self-supervised learning with class-wise reweighting to account for label imbalance, which we evaluate using the ImageNet dataset and a multi-label subset.  Our results indicate that our proposed method excels in terms of macro F1 score and overall accuracy, outperforming existing techniques.  We also demonstrate that our method can successfully handle imbalanced datasets, which presents a challenge to deep learning models.  We have shared our code and implementation details on GitHub for further exploration.  We anticipate that our work will inspire future research on resilient self-supervised learning models, which can effectively handle practical challenges in deep learning. To address this issue, a new two-stage approach is proposed, involving modality synthesis and information fusion. In the first stage, missing modality synthesis is used to create new information from available modals. This allows the model to be used with any combination of modals. The second stage involves a focus fusion module that combines the synthesized and original modality information for enhanced performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and generalization ability, particularly when dealing with previously unseen combinations of modals. The widespread adoption of Multiprotocol Label Switching has made it difficult to detect and identify Multiprotocol Label Switching Tunnels, particularly in scenarios where network traffic is not readily accessible. Research has shown that observing only the outermost packet header yields limited to no information about the inner packet, and even manually analyzing Multiprotocol Label Switching extensions reveals little about the remaining parts of the packet. To address this limitation, we introduce TNT, a network analysis tool that uses machine learning to uncover hidden Multiprotocol Label Switching tunnels. By processing a relatively small number of packets, TNT is able to make an educated guess about the inner packet's label, and subsequently use this information to make predictions about subsequent packets, effectively revealing a significant portion of the remaining Multiprotocol Label Switching extensions. We tested TNT on a real-world data set and found that it was able to reveal a remarkable 77% of the observed Multiprotocol Label Switching extensions. We examine the movement of the bag center of mass within a hadron via an effective bag potential, and our findings reveal that its trajectory is influenced by the hadron's internal motion. Utilizing the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation to represent internal motion, we derive equations governing the center of mass in the hadron's rest frame and Lab frame. In the case of a moving hadron, this internal motion induces oscillations in the center of mass. However, for very massive hadrons, these oscillations become negligible due to their minimal amplitude. A new direction of arrival estimation method utilizing a combination of external microphone and GCC-PHAT attributes is proposed. The external microphone's location serves as a key feature within the DNN. The proposed approach is tested using real-world datasets and compared with existing methods, demonstrating superior performance. Notably, this method achieves the best results when the microphone is positioned at the speaker's ear level, but it remains effective even when the microphone is positioned at a more lateral angle. The results remain robust when the signal-to-noise ratio is low, indicating that this method is well-suited for real-world applications. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial when a single microphone is available, making it an attractive solution for applications where additional microphones cannot be deployed. The experimental results also highlight the significant advantage of using multiple microphones, which can be integrated into this method to improve its accuracy. A comparative analysis of the proposed approach with other methods, such as the spatial information-based method and the external microphone-free method, is also presented. The results demonstrate that this method achieves the best performance when combined with an external microphone. Overall, this work presents a novel and efficient approach to direction of arrival estimation that is well-suited for applications with limited microphone resources. Current video conferencing systems have limited quality due to low-bandwidth constraints, a problem exacerbated by the high resolution and dynamic scene changes of modern video encoding algorithms.  Recent studies have leveraged the capabilities of neural networks to improve video compression, yet their practical use remains restricted due to various limitations, such as the requirement for high computational power and large storage capacity.  Our proposed solution, Gemino, addresses these practical concerns by introducing an efficient video compression framework suitable for real-time applications.  By combining a novel video compression algorithm with a highly optimized implementation, Gemino achieves superior performance, particularly in reducing bitrate by 20% to 40% while maintaining high video quality and comparable to established methods.  Our framework is further enhanced by the incorporation of a robust error correction mechanism that minimizes quality loss in the event of packet loss.  As a result, Gemino's effectiveness is validated through extensive testing on real-world video conferencing datasets, a process that was facilitated by the development of an open-source implementation in a widely used video encoding framework.  Our implementation enables seamless integration of Gemino into existing video conferencing systems, thereby facilitating real-world evaluation and analysis of its performance in various conditions.  Our evaluation results confirm Gemino's robustness in the face of packet loss and demonstrate its potential to deliver improved quality in the most challenging scenarios.  Our work is the first to integrate neural compression into a highly efficient video encoding algorithm, suitable for real-time applications, and to make this technology accessible to other researchers and developers.  Our open-source implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/VideoCompression.
