The organization of documents into categories plays a vital role in search engine optimization. This paper outlines a method for classifying documents into genres, a type of category that captures essential characteristics of each work. By utilizing such categories, search engines can better understand user intent and the content of documents. The proposed approach involves two stages of clustering based on sentence-level analysis. Initially, sentences are grouped according to their topic, followed by the grouping of individual document passages into a comprehensive whole, each representing a distinct genre. The ultimate goal is to achieve a balance between precision and recall in the clustering process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed clustering method in capturing meaningful genres, which can be utilized for improving search engine performance. This research contributes to enhancing search engine effectiveness, particularly in situations with limited contextual information. The associated source code is available on GitHub.

The Gravitational Wave Open Science Center's Gravity Spy platform enables users to explore and analyze data from the GWOC dataset, which includes results from the first Advanced LIGO observing run. Notably, the research also reveals that 71% of astrophysical candidates classified as glitches have multiple users' input, underscoring the importance of user participation in identifying signal contamination. Seismic interpretation is an intricate process that relies heavily on the expertise of experienced interpreters, who can take hours to manually segment complex geological structures. To alleviate this issue, we propose a new approach called Cooperative Inversion-Segmentation, which leverages a VAE-generated segmentation map and a PDE-driven optimization process to improve the segmentation process. By utilizing a VAE encoder-decoder to segment the input seismic data, we can then use a PDE framework to refine the results through a process of gradient descent. This approach enables the identification of class boundaries, which in turn allows for the optimization of the segmentation mask. By iteratively refining this segmentation map, we can successfully segment complex structures, as demonstrated by our experiments on the Sants and Kikkanjuri datasets, which showcase our approach's ability to handle intricate geological structures, diverse rock types, and noise. In comparison to PDE-based optimization alone, our CIIS approach yields superior results, up to 9% mIoU, while also demonstrating greater robustness to noise. Furthermore, our results indicate that CIIS outperforms U-Net alone, with a significant mIoU gain of up to 6%. Overall, our cooperative inversion-segmentation approach offers a promising solution for handling the complexities of seismic data segmentation. By leveraging VAE, PDE, and optimization, we can successfully improve the segmentation process, reduce the need for manual input, and achieve better results in a shorter amount of time. The objective of open-set identification is to determine if a test sample originates from a known class distribution without any knowledge of unknown classes. This process involves designing a binary classifier that can effectively distinguish known from unknown samples. A novel approach to open-set identification involves training a classifier using labeled known samples and negative examples generated from unseen classes, all by applying data augmentation techniques. This method is based on the assumption that unknown samples, when augmented, will produce lower similarity scores than genuine data. This method is particularly useful in real-world applications where the set of unknown classes cannot be determined beforehand. The trained classifier can be applied to any test sample, regardless of its origin. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through experiments on benchmark datasets. The results show that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, recall, and f-score. By integrating this approach into existing methods, we can accurately assess the likelihood of messages being social engineering attacks and produce more effective countermequots. In contrast, a model using a traditional approach might simply identify the language as suspicious without fully comprehending the underlying social dynamics. Overall, our modified Word2Vec model demonstrates superior performance over existing methods, making it a valuable tool for detecting social engineering and producing countermequots. Recent advancements in light field depth estimation have been fueled by the growing availability of high-resolution images captured by advanced imaging systems. Nonetheless, the complexity of these images poses significant challenges to current methods, particularly in cases of occlusion, where methods often struggle to produce accurate depth estimates. In response, this study introduces a novel cost builder that leverages the geometric insights of light field depth estimation to improve its performance in the presence of occlusion. By employing a two-step approach, this method initially estimates the depth of unoccluded areas using a baseline method and subsequently refines this estimate by taking into account the geometric relationships between occluded pixels and their unoccluded counterparts. Furthermore, this approach incorporates a pixel-wise confidence score to filter out unreliable estimates, demonstrating its effectiveness through its superior performance on benchmark datasets in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques.
